The Master of Art in User Experience/User Interface (UX/UI) Design is a stackable master's that combines the four-course Graduate Certificate in User Experience Design, developed by WRT, and the four-course Graduate Certificate in User Interface Design, created by ART, augmented by two additional courses.
The thirty-credit program will prepare students for meaningful careers in the burgeoning fields of UX/UI.
This online accelerated dual-focus curriculum offers students— including those with full-time jobs—a flexible path to gaining proficiency with the tools and approaches of the closely related fields of UX and UI research and design, opening a broad range of lucrative career opportunities.
Students emerge from this program as versatile professionals capable of addressing complex design challenges.
Their skills span from the intricate details of UI elements to the strategic considerations of holistic user experiences.
Armed with the knowledge of both UX and UI, graduates become adept at designing solutions that merge aesthetics, functionality, and human-centered values.
The program is unique in its emphasis on the ethical implications of research and design processes and products.

The UX Certificate nurtures an understanding of user behavior, needs, and expectations through rigorous research, ensuring accessibility and accessible design.
UX courses guide students in creating designs that prioritize inclusivity, social justice, sustainability, and user well-being.
They also offer students cutting-edge approaches to UX writing and interaction design.
The UI Design Certificate provides students with the crucial knowledge, and the technical and practical skills, to become proficient UI designers.
Students will create interface projects integrating branding, animation, patternmaking, and front-end visualizations to depict intuitive user experiences, enabling them to craft interactions that leave a lasting impact.
Students in the Master's Program are able to take UI Visual Principles for Non-designers, which helps them develop a unique approach to the design process with the user interface experience in mind (advanced designers may also select an approved elective from other URIO offerings).
The two certificates then culminate in WRT/ART 509: UX/UI Portfolio.

In this cross-listed course (WRT and ART), students integrate and apply the knowledge and skills they have gained in their UX and UI Design Certificate courses to create compelling, effective, polished portfolios that demonstrate their expertise to potential employers and clients.
Additionally, the course will focus on professionalization for careers in UX, UI, and related design fields.
Graduates of this program will have the capability to examine how individuals navigate real-life scenarios, empowering them to enhance experiences by creating new design-centered connections.
They will possess the abilities to recognize limitations and openings for enhancing interactions between objects, systems—whether virtual or physical—as well as the people who interact with them.
In an ever-evolving technological landscape, the Master of Arts in UX/UI Design equips students to stand at the forefront of innovation, transcending traditional boundaries between the two fields.
Graduates leave prepared to meet industry demands and set new standards that enrich the lives of users, making a positive impact on society.

Strategy 1 in the Agenda for Change is deeply embedded in the goals and learning outcomes of this program.
The Master's in UX/UI emphasizes the application of ethical, collaborative design practices to solve real-world problems, focusing on inclusive design, design justice, person-first design, and designing for the social good.
Students will learn to engage in design processes that prioritize the needs and perspectives of diverse user populations.
By understanding the principles of inclusive design, they will acquire the ability to create solutions that cater to a wide range of users, ensuring accessibility and usability for all.

Through a combination of theoretical concepts, case studies, and practical exercises, students will gain an understanding of the ethical challenges faced by user experience designers and develop strategies to create user- centered and ethically sound designs.
Students will explore UX as a research and development method, especially as it relates to inclusive design and design justice.
Students will learn about foundational concepts in UX design, including terminology, history, and evolution of the field.
Using a critical lens, students will investigate issues of social justice, equity, sustainability, accessibility, and inclusion.
WRT 502: UX Research and Methods is an introduction to methods, research design, and data analysis in user experience projects, and aims to prepare professionals for designing, conducting, analyzing, and reporting their own user research studies.

This course will train students in how to determine the best methods and metrics for their projects, as well as design studies for effective data collection.
This course will also teach students how to communicate research results for decision-making purposes to a variety of stakeholders.
Students in this course will gain hands-on practice at every phase of the user research process, from identifying design problems or questions to developing their own test protocols, recruiting users, conducting user tests, and analyzing their results.
WRT 503: UX and Microcopy Writing is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the role and impact of effective writing in user-centered design.
Through a combination of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students will develop the skills necessary to create clear, concise, and engaging microcopy for digital interfaces and interactions.
WRT 504: Interaction Design focuses on the process of rapid, iterative design that keeps real people at the heart of creating content—a philosophy and design approach known as human-centered design.

Students in this course will learn agile design workflows, conduct rapid prototyping and wireframing, and share reflections on the process and results of user research meaningfully for public and industry audiences.
Students will gain hands-on, applied knowledge of the human-centered design process by creating their own design and refining it based on user feedback.

ART 505: UI Design: Styling and Prototyping introduces students to the theory and practice of user interface design, focusing on visual communication tools and skills to facilitate prototyping.
Students will acquire a knowledge of the UI design thinking process, centering on the user's visual experience, which is crucial to how users interact with an interface.
Students will learn how to collaborate as a visual designer in creating interactive screen-based interfaces for websites and apps, creating visual components while considering their interactive properties, look and feel, responsiveness and interactivity and recognizing the multiple human factors, audiences and contexts that govern their design decisions.
ART 506: UI Motion Design introduces motion design in user experience within a framework of the three foundational principles of communication, orientation, and correlation.
Students will learn how motion design can complement visual affordances to provide users with more meaningful experiences and interactions.
It explores motion design as a sequence of movements that affects the user’s perception of any interface a user interacts with.

ART 507: UI Icon Design introduces and develops the skills needed to conceptualize and design icons for user interfaces.
The context, design and application of UI icons will be critiqued based on the effectiveness and appropriateness of the design language.
Students will learn to generate UI icon sets through a process that explores visual rhetoric and shape form creation through a logical visual process.
This course provides an overview of the nature and purpose of icons in user interfaces, their key characteristics, and aesthetic rules commonly used in websites and apps.
ART 508: UI Information Visualization Design focuses on the design, creation, understanding, application, and evaluation of information visualization for user interfaces.
Students will learn strategies and techniques to organize, visualize and communicate information and how to implement them on multiple platforms.

Students will gain an understanding of the importance of the interface focusing on users and the graphical depictions of complex information for more efficient and effective processing, leading to faster and more accurate results.The course reflects upon the many ways in which information design is carried out to improve the student’s own design process, and to convey meaning from information, with the primary focus placed on educating the viewer through their visualization experiences.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report 2023-2024-02 - Proposed amendments to Appendix G Faculty Senate - March 28, 2024 Rationale: The primary change proposed relates to increasing clarity in the reference to Policy #80-1 in Appendix G.
When the Faculty Senate authorized migrating administrative policies previously listed in Appendix G to the Administrative Policies website, an error was introduced wherein Policy #80-1 regarding Faculty Senate jurisdiction over policies was inadvertently deleted.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee found no evidence that the Faculty Senate ever rescinded the missing Policy, gave an informational report on this matter to the Faculty Senate on October 19, 2023, and reposted a link to the policy in Appendix G along with a brief explanation about what had occurred.
Because Policy #80-1 codifies a power and duty of the Faculty Senate relating to the approval of administrative policies, it is appropriate and important to include not only a link to the policy in this Appendix but also clear details about the content of the policy and the codified role of the Faculty Senate in the administrative policy development and approval process.

Additional changes aim to 1) accurately reflect the relationship between academic policies and collective bargaining agreements and state and federal statutes and regulations, 2) clarify the nature of the University Manual as the official policy document where policies are not only described but also codified through legislative processes, and 3) correct an error in fact (it is not the President of the Faculty Senate, but rather the entire body of the Faculty Senate that has the authority to jointly own policies).
Proposed changes to Appendix G: University Policies In recognition that the University Manual has been created through the framework of shared governance between the university faculty and administration under the University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees, it is the source of information regarding the structure, rights, regulations, and practices that govern university life.
The Manual is considered to be the official university policy document articulating shared governance and, as such, takes precedence over other internal policy statements inconsistent or conflicting with the Manual.

Academic policies, with the exception of those mandated by collective bargaining agreements or by government at state or federal levels statutes or regulations, are legislated by Faculty Senate and Presidential action, and are articulated and codified in the various Chapters and Appendices of this Manual.
Administrative policies are set forth within the framework of this Appendix and maintained by the Office of the Vice President of Administration and Finance, with oversight by the Administrative Policy Committee.
Administrative policies with provisions that fall under Faculty Senate jurisdiction also require approval by the Page 1 of 2 FSEC Report 2023-2024-02 Bill #23-24-20

Faculty Senate.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee shall determine if some or all of the provisions of an administrative policy fall under Faculty Senate jurisdiction.
Policy #80-1 (“Establishing Administrative Policy”) Research and intellectual property (IP) policies are academic and administrative policies set forth in Section 4 of this Appendix maintained by the Office of the Vice President for Research and Economic Development.
Although many research policies are academic in nature affecting the faculty as a whole, many other research policies are treated as administrative in nature, mandated by requirements of federal and state granting authorities.
SECTION 2 — University of Rhode Island Policy on Policies The University of Rhode Island Policy on Policies (Policy #01.101), owned jointly by the Vice President for Administration and Finance and the Faculty Senate President, provides definitions of Administrative and Academic policies and provides guidance on the development and approval of those policies.
In addition, the policy provides information regarding regular review, promulgation, policy repositories, and archiving.

Detailed information about the University of Rhode Island Policy on Policies can be found on the Administrative Policies website: https://web.uri.edu/policies/.
When the Faculty Senate authorized migrating administrative policies previously listed in Appendix G to the Administrative Policies website, an error was introduced wherein Policy #80-1 regarding Faculty Senate jurisdiction over policies was inadvertently deleted.
Since there is no evidence the Faculty Senate ever rescinded the missing Policy, it has been reposted here: Policy #80-1, “Establishing Administrative Policy,” revised (#21-22-24) (#21-22-25) (IFSR #2023-2024-3) Page 2 of 2 FSEC Report 2023-2024-02 Bill #23-24-20

Methods of Instruction The CAC has adopted the following definitions of methods of instruction: Definitions for Methods of Instruction Revision of definitions in the CAC's Three Hundred and Seventh Report (October 13, 1993) Lecture: A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small- group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.
Laboratory: In-class applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
Recitation: Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
Studio: In-class, supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which facuity instruct, assist, and critique. 2

Seminar: Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20* students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.
Independent Study: One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities.
Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
Practicum: Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice.
Includes clinics, internships, ex tern ships, student teaching, field experiences.
May include regular class meetings.
Workshop: Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.
Online: A course that is delivered entirely online. (CAC policy includes possibility of a required organizational session, etc.) SECTIONI Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Facuity Senate A.

Matt Wei, GSO Committee Overview Structure The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (CRCA) consists of six faculty senators and five non-senator research-active faculty.
The Vice President for Research and Economic Development (VPRED) is an ex officio (non-voting) member of the committee.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee appoints six senators and the VPRED appoints five research-active non-senators to the committee.
The CRCA also comprises a subcommittee, the Competitive Grants Subcommittee.
The CRCA was restructured in 2024 to include non- senators, expanding the committee from 6 to 11 faculty members.
Charge The full committee serves as the representative voice of the university community in all matters related to research, creative, and scholarly activities.

It seeks to improve the environment for research at URI in all ways possible.
The committee oversees the following areas related to research: Advocacy of Research and Creative Activities The committee is to promote a comprehensive understanding of the notion of research, creative, and scholarly work in order to enhance the well-being of all such work at URI; seek to identify all challenges that do or could hinder research, creative, and scholarly efforts at URI and provide recommendations to correct them; review and recommend policies for the management of research affairs at URI and serve as the advisory committee for the Vice President for Research and Economic Development; upon request, advise all campus groups and offices on matters relating to research, creative, and scholarly work.

Library and Open Access The committee acts as a liaison between the University Libraries (Library) and the faculty as a whole and advise the Library on matters of general faculty concern; consult with the Library faculty on long-range needs of the Library and the adequacy of budget provisions to meet those needs; serve in an advisory capacity to the Faculty Senate regarding the implementation and interpretation of the University of Rhode Island Open-Access Policy, resolving disputes concerning the interpretation and application of the policy and recommending changes of the policy to the Faculty Senate.

Competitive Grants Subcommittee The subcommittee solicits proposals from the faculty and awards, on a competitive basis, financial support for a “Faculty Development” program (using guidelines developed together with the full committee) to support faculty salary and fellowships, student support, operating expenses, travel, and equipment; advises the Vice President fo r Research and Economic Development concerning the allocation among faculty, on a competitive basis , of financial support for a “Proposal Development” program (using guidelines developed by the Vice President for Research and Economic Development in consultation with the full committee) to support faculty salary and fellowships, student support, operating expenses, travel, and equipment. 2025 –26 Activities The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (CRCA) membership included 6 senators and 3 non- senators.
The committee met regularly throughout Academic Year 2025–2026 to address key issues impacting the University’s research and creative enterprise.

The committee’s work this year focused on three primary areas: (1) supporting faculty success in a shifting federal funding landscape, (2) identifying and addressing challenges facing graduate students, and (3) evaluating and redefining the committee’s role, structure, and alignment within the University.
Throughout the academic year, CRCA engaged in regular, productive exchanges with VPRED Bethany Jenkins, who provided timely and transparent updates on the evolving federal research landscape, institutional responses, and emerging challenges affecting faculty.
These discussions were both informative and collaborative, with committee members sharing on-the-ground perspectives that informed committee discussions and the institution's understanding of research-related challenges for faculty.
CRCA also contribut ed to the interview process for the next AVP of Research Development.
Below is an overview of what was discussed and planned during this period: 1.
Faculty Support in a Changing Research Environment A central theme throughout the year was the evolving federal funding landscape and its implications for faculty research productivity and evaluation.

Early in the year, the committee identified the need for clearer guidance on promotion and tenure expectations in light of funding uncertainties.
This led to discussions and initial drafting efforts to develop peer-review and evaluation guidance that accounts for structural shifts in funding availability.
During the winter, the committee engaged directly with Sue Adams, Vice Provost for Academic and Faculty Initiatives.
These conversations reinforced the need for flexibility and a more holistic approach to faculty evaluation.
The committee also explored the proposed “Achievement Relative to Opportunity” supplement, ultimately determining that existing mechanisms, particularly the applicant statement, were sufficient and more appropriate for contextualizing faculty contributions. 2.
Graduate Student Support The committee identified graduate student support as a priority area, particularly amid the rising cost-of-living concerns and housing challenges.
Discussions highlighted the intersection of financial constraints, housing availability, and the recruitment/retention of graduate students.

In December, CRCA hosted Ellen Reynolds, Vice President for Student Affairs, and Thomas Cooley, Associate Vice President for Student Affairs, to discuss graduate housing initiatives and broader financial challenges facing students.
Key takeaways included the importance of transparent communication with prospective students about the cost of living and the potential need to revisit graduate stipend structures, including budgeting practices for externally funded grants.
The committee also emphasized the importance of continued engagement with Graduate School leadership and plans to revisit these discussions in the coming academic year to further develop actionable recommendations. 3.
Committee Structure, Scope, and Strategic Alignment A portion of the committee’s work this year focused on a critical evaluation of its structure, charge, and institutional role.
Early discussions identified the need to formalize term limits for non -senator members and to more clearly define the committee’s scope, particularly regarding creative activities, intellectual property, and its interface with other university entities.

These conversations reflected a broader recognition that the current structure does not fully position CRCA to meet the evolving needs of the research enterprise.
Building on this assessment, the committee discussed potential restructuring to strengthen its impact and clarify its role in institutional governance.
Two primary models were explored: (a) a joint committee operating in formal partnership between the Faculty Senate and the Division of Research, or (b) a committee housed within the Division of Research with formal Faculty Senate representation.
Both models would more intentionally position CRCA as a strategic, bidirectional conduit for faculty input on rese arch-related issues and as a responsive advisory body to institutional leadership.
Preliminary discussions with Bethany Jenkins and the Faculty Senate Executive Committee indicated openness to advancing a restructuring proposal.
Given the significance of these changes, the committee determined that further development, stakeholder input, and alignment with Faculty Senate processes are needed.

As such, formal proposals and decisions have been intentionally deferred to the next academic year to ensure thoughtful planning and broad engagement.
For continuity and efficiency, d rafted documents developed this year will be carried forward and shared with next year’s committee, providing a foundation for continued refinement and timely progress. 4.
Competitive Grants Subcommittee See subcommittee report. 5.
Key Themes and Looking Ahead Across all areas of work, several consistent themes emerged: ● The need for adaptable faculty evaluation frameworks in response to external funding variability ● The importance of strengthening institutional support for graduate students ● The value of clear, coordinated structures connecting faculty governance and research administration ● Increasing demand for internal research support mechanisms 6.
F&A Report As part of the CRCA charge, an annual F&A report is typically included in the committee’s end-of-year report to the Faculty Senate.
However, the most recent FY25 data currently available are already approximately 11 months old, raising questions about the usefulness and timeliness of reporting those figures this spring.

In addition, changes in the University’s budget structure have limited the level of detail available for reporting.
While the business office can still provide F&A distributions and proportional research administration assessments by college, other research -related expenses are now aggregated with broader non -research operational costs, limiting the ability to provide the same level of reporting detail as in prior years.
Given both the timing and reporting limitations, the committee believes the Senate would be better served by shifting the F&A reporting

cycle to the fall, when more current and complete data are available. The committee plans to revisit this issue as part of its broader restructuring discussions in the coming academic year. Conclusion CRCA played an important role this year as a forum for identifying emerging challenges, facilitating communication between faculty and research leadership, and laying the groundwork for structural improvements. The committee is well -positioned to build on this work in the coming year, with a focus on implementing changes that strengthen the research environment and support faculty and student success.
